div.head: VI Atr 47
div.ab: ⁊ þæt hy wydewan ⁊ steopcild to oft ne ahwænan, ac georne hy gladian.
And þæt hi wuduwan ⁊ steopcild to oft ne ahwǽnan, ac georne hi gladian.
⁊ þæt hy wydewan ⁊ steopcild to oft ne ahwænan ac georne hi gladian.
And þæt hy wydewan and steopcild to oft ne ahwænan, ac georne hy gladian.
Und dass sie Wittwen und Waisen nicht zu oft belästigen, sondern sie gerne erfreuen.
And that they do not too often distress widows and orphans, but gladly make them happy.
And that they should not be constantly oppressing the widow and the orphan, but that they should diligently cheer them.
And that widows and orphans are not to be continually persecuted, but instead uplifted.

note.seg: Vielleicht direkt aus Exodus 22, 22; allein die Worte stimmen zu Ælfred; vgl. Gl Witwe 1. 7. Jedenfalls stammt die Zusammenstellung mit Fremden (48) aus Bibel oder daraus Abgeleitetem. Als Vertreter der Volkspflicht schützt neben der Kirche der Königsfrieden (s. d. Gl 9a) die Schwachen; s. Gl Waise

Perhaps directly from Exodus 22, 22; but the words agree with Ælfred; cf. Gl Witwe 1. 7. At any rate the association with strangers (48) comes from the Bible or from something derived from it. As representative of the public duty, the king’s peace (see that word in Gl 9a) protects the weak alongside the Church; see Gl Waise
Liebermann suggests that this clause may have been derived from Exodus Ch. 22, v. 22; cf. Wulfstan, p. 119.
